title: AI current lawsuits
author: Exotic-Ad515
selftext:
Hey just curious if any of you have been following the lawsuits pertaining to AI use. Any work produced by AI has no copyright protection. Which means that anyone can rip off your game and resell it without issue. 

Thaler v. Perlmutter 

If you use AI as a tool, you might be okay. If you strictly use prompts, you don't own your product. This pertains to code and assets.

comments.author: Kid-Icky-
comments.body:
This is overstating Thaler v. Perlmutter pretty badly.

The ruling says purely AI-generated material without human authorship isn't copyrightable. It does not say "use AI anywhere in your game and your entire game becomes public domain."

Human-written code, story, dialogue, level design, edited assets, and creative arrangement can still be copyrighted. Even AI-generated material can become protectable to the extent a human substantially modifies it.

So yes, raw prompt-to-output assets may lack copyright protection. No, that does not mean someone can just copy and resell your entire game "without issue".

replies.author: Kid-Icky-
replies.body:
I read it. And if someone genuinely prompts 100% of a game with literally no meaningful human authorship anywhere, then yes, they may have little or no copyright protection over those generated elements.

So yeah, one-shotting *"Make GT6, make no mistakes"* might have no protection. But so what? I don't think that applies to almost anyone here.

Most "prompted" games still involve human selection, arrangement, editing, integration, debugging, and other creative decisions that can be protected. Thaler was about a work where the AI was explicitly claimed as the sole author.

Your post was far too broad for what the ruling actually stated.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
There are a lot of wrong assumptions being made here.

It was already confirmed by courts that works with sufficient human direction, arrangement or creative control all are eligible for copyright protection.

Now what does this mean in practice?

If you throw a single prompt into AI and try to copyright the result, you can't. This assumes very little human direction (with rare exceptions perhaps if your prompt is long/detailed enough.) On the other hand, if you are iterating with the AI, testing features, directing it through multiple prompts (and frankly any game that turns out even remotely good using AI is going to involve thousands of iterations this way)... You absolutely have provided enough creative direction, arrangement, and creative control to copyright the final work. It's not even particularly close.

They ruled that a stupid collage was considered a protected work and all the guy did was take like 20 different AI generated images that he hadn't edited at all, and arranged them on a canvas.

This may vary for certain other countries. But copyright and trademark are fairly nebulous once you start crossing international borders anyway.

So you don't have to go and write 20% of your code to ensure it stays protected (at least within the bounds of how much code can actually be protected). That's not how this works.

comments.author: dreadpirater
comments.body:
As someone who's been an artist and taught artists for 25 years...   COPYRIGHT WASN'T PROTECTING ANYBODY IN THIS THREAD WITH OR WITHOUT THE AI QUESTION.   That's not to say it doesn't cover your work or shouldn't.  But the U.S. laws aren't going to DO anything to protect you anyway.  

The reason is - copyright is established in federal law and so any suit about it has to be brought in federal court.   If you're not willing and able to drop $50k on a lawsuit to defend your work, it doesn't matter what the copyright law SAYS...   you can't benefit from it.   It's a HUGE problem for small artists, and it's come about because the BIG artists like Disney owned the politicians who wrote the current laws...  so they're great at protecting you if you have a building full of lawyers and useless if you don't.   

Also, mechanical principles can't be copyrighted anyway...   So the literal source code and the text of your dialog boxes is likely the only thing in your program that IS covered by copyright - someone can hand all your screenshots to Claude and say "Clone this app" and that's perfectly legal.   The only protection your app has against copycats is and has always been - is it hard to make?   If you're doing something simple, you'll be cloned.  If you're putting real thought into it, then it at least takes real thought to copy you.   The other distinguishing factor is the business around your application - writing code has ALWAYS been the easy part of software development.   The thing that separates the billionaires from the 'went broke paying for my web hosting' folks isn't the software itself, usually, it's your skill at marketing and supporting it.  Claude can't copy that, yet, either, so that's where you need to put your energy if you want to last in a market niche.  

Stressing about copyright law is a waste of energy if you're not grossing a million dollars.  You can't afford the lawsuit anyway, so don't worry about what the law says.
